recipe: v10 renames state.gl to state.renderer, because the renderer may be WebGPURenderer. gl still resolves but logs a deprecation warning. If you only ever want WebGLRenderer, import from '@react-three/fiber/legacy' and the warning stops.

state.clock is gone in v10. Timing comes off the RAF timer: state.delta (seconds), state.elapsed (seconds since first frame), state.time (RAF ms), state.frame (counter). clock.getElapsedTime() becomes state.elapsed.

v10: any useFrame job with { phase: 'render' } skips the default render for that root. Numeric priority > 0 still takes over but is deprecated, and the migration guide warns it can double-render with your own render() call; use { phase: 'render' }.
replaces: useFrame(({ gl, scene, camera }) => gl.render(scene, camera), 1)
_original_recipe: Biggest silent v10 breakage: in v9 only priority>0 disabled the default render. In v10 registering ANY job in the render phase does. Old priority code that also calls render() double-renders. Use { phase: 'render' }.
_review_reason: v10 frame-loop doc says numeric priority>0 still takes over (deprecated); 'always double-renders' overstated

recipe: Peer floors differ sharply. r3f v9: three >=0.156, react >=19.0. r3f v10: three >=0.185.0, react >=19.0 <19.3. On three r181-r184 v10 will not install at all; bump three alongside R3F.
_original_recipe: Version floors differ sharply. v9 peers: three >=0.156, react >=19 <19.3. v10 peers: three >=0.185.0, react >=19.0 <19.3. On three r181-r184 v10 will not install at all; bump three alongside.
_review_reason: wrong v9 react range: v9 peers react >=19.0 with no <19.3 ceiling (v10 migration table)

recipe: React Native left the package in v10: '@react-three/fiber/native' is now the separately versioned '@react-three/native'. In v9 the native entry and expo peer deps still ship inside @react-three/fiber.

v10 alpha.3 deletes Canvas props legacy, linear, flat, colorSpace, toneMapping, and the matching RootState keys. Push them into the renderer bag: renderer={{ toneMapping: NoToneMapping }}. ColorManagement.enabled is now unconditionally true.

textureColorSpace survives v10 but is no longer a top-level Canvas prop. It moved into ColorManagementConfig, intersected into GLProps and RendererProps, so pass it inside gl={{...}} or renderer={{...}}.

Default shadow type changed in v10 alpha.3 from PCFSoftShadowMap to PCFShadowMap, tracking three r182. The shadows aliases 'percentage' and 'soft' still resolve to PCFShadowMap but warn. Expect visibly harder default shadow edges.

v10 parents the default camera to the scene so camera-attached lights and HUD meshes render. Consequence: every index in scene.children shifts by one, so scene.children[0] now returns the camera, not your first mesh.
replaces: scene.children[0] to reach the first rendered object

recipe: v10 deprecates <color attach="background" /> for a Canvas background prop taking a CSS color, hex number, HDR/EXR url, or an HDRI preset name ('sunset'), plus an object form with backgroundBlurriness and environmentIntensity.

v10 ships three entries: '@react-three/fiber' (WebGL default, WebGPU-ready), '/legacy' (WebGLRenderer only, smaller, no deprecation warnings), '/webgpu' (WebGPURenderer plus TSL hooks). v9 has one entry. Match your test-renderer import to it.
_review_reason: tags only: entry points are a tooling/bundling concern

recipe: v10 defaults events.frameTimedRaycasts to true: pointer-move raycasts are deferred to frame start and processed once per frame, not once per DOM event. v9 raycast on every move event.
v10 alpha.3 stops re-exporting act; import it from 'react'. In v9 both work, and v9's own migration already recommended React's act since it is the same function.

v9.7.0 hardened the reconciler against react-dom: keyed child reorder no longer desyncs the internal map, removed pierced props reset on the pierced target rather than the root, event priorities match react-dom, reconciler schedules via microtasks.

v9.7.0 (ported into the v10 alpha) makes commitUpdate sync instance.props wholesale. The behaviour people notice: imperative mutations now survive a re-render instead of being stomped by re-applied defaults, and removed props stop lingering.
Pin drei by r3f major: drei 10.x peers @react-three/fiber ^9.0.0 and three >=0.159. drei 11 alpha peers fiber >=10.0.0-0, three >=0.185, react >=19.0 <19.3. They do not cross-install.

During the alpha no drei release declares support for fiber ^10, so package managers may warn or refuse to resolve r3f v10 with drei. Ordinary drei usage is expected to work because v10's default entry keeps the v9 surface.

v9 removed hardcoded prop exports: MeshProps becomes ThreeElements['mesh']. The Node/Object3DNode/MaterialNode/LightNode helpers collapsed into ThreeElement<typeof X>. JSX types are now generated from three's API rather than hand-maintained.

Since v9 declare custom elements by augmenting the module, never global JSX.IntrinsicElements, which React 19 deprecated. declare module '@react-three/fiber' { interface ThreeElements { customElement: ThreeElement<typeof CustomElement> } }.
replaces: declare global { namespace JSX { interface IntrinsicElements { ... } } }

recipe: v9 inherits StrictMode from the parent react-dom root. Remove the redundant inner <StrictMode> you needed in v8. If something worked in v8 and fails now, StrictMode has flushed out a real side effect.
_review_reason: tags only: StrictMode is React, not GPU

recipe: v9 removed automatic sRGB conversion of texture props; built-in materials handle color textures like vanilla three, so data textures stop being corrupted. For custom materials tag them yourself: texture-colorSpace={THREE.SRGBColorSpace}.
replaces: relying on r3f to force sRGB on every texture prop

recipe: v10 alpha.4 makes frameloop root-scoped: each Canvas owns its mode and pending frames, so a demand Canvas no longer freezes an always sibling. State-bound invalidate/advance target one root; the stateless exports still fan out globally.

v10 deprecates the v9 globals: addEffect becomes useFrame(cb, { phase: 'start' }), addAfterEffect becomes { phase: 'finish' }, addTail becomes scheduler.onIdle. invalidate and advance are unchanged. The legacy ones only receive a raw RAF timestamp.

Small v10 alpha.3 breakages that break a build collectively: advance() narrowed to (timestamp: number), Mutable

now uses -readonly, ObjectMap became generic, TextureEntry is no longer exported, Canvas CSS is width/height 100%.

Treat every v10 feature as provisional: the maintainers say to consider all of it experimental and subject to change or removal. useTextures is flagged EXPERIMENTAL and already changed shape once (textures became all; addMultiple and friends removed).

R3F is a React renderer for three.js, not a wrapper. <boxGeometry /> is new THREE.BoxGeometry(), constructed on first mount only. A camelCased element resolves against the extend catalogue, so unknown names throw rather than render nothing.
source_name: r3f docs: How does it work?

recipe: args is the constructor argument array and only the constructor's. Changing args after mount reconstructs the object from scratch, dropping GPU state and re-running side effects, so never derive args from animated values.
source_name: r3f docs: Objects, properties and constructor arguments

recipe: Never build THREE instances inline in JSX; they are recreated every render. position={[1,2,3]} beats position={new Vector3(1,2,3)}, and <sphereGeometry args={[1,16,16]} /> beats geometry={new SphereGeometry(...)}.
source_name: r3f docs: Objects, properties and constructor arguments

recipe: Any prop whose target has .set() accepts set's arguments: color="hotpink", position={[1,2,3]}. Targets with setScalar accept a number: scale={1}. Passing an existing Vector3/Euler/Matrix copies it via .copy(); materials and geometries overwrite instead.
source_name: r3f docs: Objects, properties and constructor arguments

recipe: Dash-case pierces into nested properties: rotation-x={1}, shadow-camera-far={50}, material-uniforms-resolution-value={[512,512]}. It saves an object allocation and mutates in place rather than replacing the sub-object.
source_name: r3f docs: Objects, properties and constructor arguments

recipe: attach binds a non-Object3D child to a parent property and unbinds on unmount. Anything extending Material or BufferGeometry auto-attaches, so typing attach="material" is redundant. Pierce with attach="attributes-position", index arrays with attach="material-0".
source_name: r3f docs: Objects, properties and constructor arguments

recipe: When the parent needs explicit add/remove rather than assignment, pass attach a function returning its own cleanup: attach={(parent, self) => (parent.add(self), () => parent.remove(self))}. attach is fixed on first set and ignored if updated later.

<primitive object={obj} /> adopts an existing instance and is how a loaded GLTF scene enters the tree. Two rules: three silently removes an object from its first parent if added twice, so clone; and primitive never disposes what it carries.
source_name: r3f docs: Objects, properties and constructor arguments

recipe: R3F calls .dispose() on every unmounted object it created. If the asset is cached or globally shared, that is a use-after-free: set dispose={null}, which applies to the whole subtree when placed on a parent group.
replaces: manual disposal bookkeeping in useEffect cleanup
source_name: r3f docs: Objects, properties and constructor arguments

recipe: extend adds classes to the JSX catalogue. Prefer v9's factory form, const Controls = extend(OrbitControls), over extend({ OrbitControls }): it returns a component, so a library's element cannot collide with a userland declaration of the same name.
replaces: extend({ OrbitControls }) plus a ThreeElements augmentation

recipe: The reconciler has not auto-imported the THREE namespace since v8. extend(THREE) is convenient but defeats tree-shaking; extend({ Mesh, BoxGeometry, MeshStandardMaterial }) keeps the bundle granular, and react-three-babel can generate that automatically.

ShaderMaterial's uniforms object is kept stable: a new uniforms prop is merged into the existing target, never swapped, preserving three's uniform caching. So mutating the object you passed does nothing; mutate ref.current.uniforms.x.value instead.
replaces: keeping a useMemo'd uniforms object and mutating it per frame
source_name: r3f docs: Objects, properties and constructor arguments

recipe: A ref here holds the three.js instance, not a DOM node, and mutating it is the sanctioned fast path rather than an escape hatch. Pair mutations with the usual three flags: .needsUpdate = true, .updateProjectionMatrix().

Propagation is not the DOM's. The event goes to the nearest object, bubbles its ancestors, then to the next nearest, so objects are transparent by default. stopPropagation() also blocks objects behind, and fires their pointerout during the call.

Pointer capture adds the capturing object to the hit result rather than replacing it, so hit objects still receive the event first. setPointerCapture/releasePointerCapture live on event.target only, never on the Object3D.

Raycasting only runs while the user interacts. If the camera moves a hoverable under a still cursor, no hover fires. Call state.events.update() to replay the last pointer event, e.g. when camera.matrixWorld changes.

If overlay gizmos render on top via depth tricks but lose hit tests to geometry in front, v10 adds userData.interactivePriority. Prioritised objects sort before unprioritised ones, above the existing portal/layer priority and distance.

createRoot(canvas) drops react-dom and react-use-measure from the bundle, but it is not responsive: call root.configure({ size }) yourself on resize and opt into events explicitly. configure() must run before render(); await it when gl is an async factory (e.g. WebGPU).
_original_recipe: createRoot(canvas) drops react-dom and react-use-measure from the bundle, but you own resizing and must opt into events explicitly. configure() must be awaited before render(), and again on every resize.
_review_reason: overstated: canvas.mdx says awaiting configure() is only required for an async gl factory; resize calls configure({ size }) unawaited

recipe: Every r3f hook reads context, so calling useThree next to <Canvas> rather than inside it crashes. Split the component: the hook belongs in a child rendered by Canvas, not in the component that renders Canvas.

onUpdate is a reserved prop, not an event: it fires whenever the instance receives fresh props, which is where flags like needsUpdate belong. Since v9.7.0 reserved props like onUpdate and dispose actually update on re-render.

Removing a prop resets it to the class default. Before v10 alpha.5 any class whose constructor takes arguments (every material, geometry and camera) got 0 instead, so a removed color turned black. Symptom of an unpinned older alpha.

v10 adds fromRef and once for props that previously needed an effect. target={fromRef(targetRef)} resolves after the sibling mounts, optionally through a transform; rotateX={once(Math.PI/2)} applies a geometry method on mount only, not every render.

Per-frame work goes in useFrame and mutates refs. setState per frame routes a number through React's scheduler and re-renders the subtree for nothing. The same rule covers fast pointer events: assign ref.current.position.x, do not setX.
delta is seconds since the last frame. position.x += 0.1 runs at a different speed on a 144Hz display than on 60Hz; position.x += delta does not. Same for lerp factors you intend to be time-based.

If a store value changes at 60fps, never subscribe to it reactively; useSelector/useStore re-render the component every frame. Read it imperatively inside useFrame: api.getState().x. Reactive subscription is fine for values that change on user action.

Any new THREE.Vector3/Color/Matrix inside useFrame allocates 60 times a second and eventually stalls on GC. Hoist one instance to module or component scope and .set() it: ref.current.position.lerp(vec.set(x,y,z), 0.1).

If the same geometry or material appears in a map(), hoist it. Every material compiles and every geometry is processed on creation. useMemo inside the component, or module scope if it never depends on props.

Materials or colors created outside <Canvas> rely on THREE.ColorManagement for sRGB hex/CSS color conversion. It is on by default in modern three (r152+); only set THREE.ColorManagement.enabled = true at module scope if an older three or legacy setting disabled it.
_original_recipe: A material or color constructed outside the Canvas context misses r3f's color handling, so enable THREE.ColorManagement.enabled = true at module scope when you hoist them. Otherwise hex and CSS colors will not convert from sRGB.
_review_reason: stale: ColorManagement.enabled has defaulted to true since three r152; recipe implies you must always set it

recipe: Each mesh is a draw call. Beyond a few hundred similar objects, instance them; a thousand is the hard ceiling to aim under. <instancedMesh args={[null, null, count]} /> plus setMatrixAt in an effect and instanceMatrix.needsUpdate.

If the scene comes to rest, frameloop="demand" renders only on detected prop changes. Anything that mutates (camera controls, tweens) is invisible to React, so call invalidate() yourself. drei's controls already do.
replaces: always-on render loop for static scenes

recipe: invalidate() is a flag requesting one frame, not a render call; calling it five times does not render five times. Starting a synchronous animation right after it visibly jumps, so invalidate first and start the animation in the next rAF.

v10 details: only demand roots accumulate invalidations, pending frames are capped at 60 per root and decrement one per rendered frame, and invalidate(state, frames, stackFrames) with stackFrames true adds instead of replacing.

regress() alone changes nothing. It only moves state.performance.current toward min for the debounce window; your app must read current and act, e.g. multiply dpr by it. Wire regress to controls' change event.

Toggling stages with conditional mounting recompiles shaders and reinitialises buffers each time. Prefer <Stage1 visible={stage===1} />, keeping objects resident. Mount/unmount only when memory, not latency, is the constraint.

When one interaction constructs hundreds of expensive three objects, wrap the setState in startTransition; React distributes the work across frames instead of one long jank. Canvases run in concurrent mode by default since v8.

Never hand-roll a loader in useEffect+useState; every instance refetches and reparses. useLoader caches on the URL, so the same asset resolves to the same object everywhere in the tree. gltfjsx output relies on that sharing.

For progressive quality, nest Suspense and use the low-res model as the fallback for the high-res one. The outer boundary shows the spinner, the inner one shows real geometry while the heavy asset streams in.

Select from useThree to avoid needless re-renders: useThree(s => s.camera) re-renders only when the default camera swaps. Reactivity stops at the store; useThree(s => s.camera.zoom) never updates because three internals are not observed.
replaces: const { camera } = useThree() in a frequently-rendering component

recipe: v10 throttles per job: useFrame(runAI, { fps: 20 }). The job runs at most once per RAF and never catches up by firing twice. drop:false keeps interval accounting aligned for simulations; drop:true (default) discards missed intervals.

For conditional per-frame work in v10, pass { enabled: isActive } rather than returning early inside the callback. A disabled job stays registered but the scheduler skips it entirely, costing no frame budget.

Animation libraries with their own loop (react-spring/three, framer-motion) animate outside React and cost no re-render: <a.mesh position-x={x} />. Otherwise lerp/damp toward a target inside useFrame.

useThree returns the root zustand store's state and is reactive to store changes such as resize. For fresh values outside the render cycle, grab get from the store and call get() rather than closing over state.

Swap defaults through the store rather than the Canvas prop when it must happen at runtime: const set = useThree(s => s.set); set({ camera: new OrthographicCamera(...) }). drei's makeDefault does exactly this for cameras and controls.

viewport is three.js units at the camera's distance, size is CSS pixels; they are not interchangeable and viewport is not gl.getViewport. Use viewport.getCurrentViewport(camera, target) when the object is not at the origin.

useLoader suspends, so the result is guaranteed non-null in the body and you never branch on undefined. Fallback and error handling belong to the parent Suspense and error boundary. It is built on suspend-react.

Signature is useLoader(Loader, url, extensions, onProgress). The third argument configures the loader instance, which is where DRACOLoader is wired. An array of urls loads in parallel and returns an array.
v9 lets useLoader take a loader instance, not just a class, so you can pool and pre-configure one loader across components: const loader = new GLTFLoader(); useLoader(loader, url).

If the URL is signed or per-request it defeats the URL-keyed cache. v10 adds a fifth cacheKey argument, mirrored on preload and clear: useLoader(GLTFLoader, signedUrl, undefined, undefined, '/model.glb').

Mutating or disposing a useLoader result mutates it for every consumer, since the cache hands back the same object. Clone before you change anything, or set dispose={null}. useLoader.preload(Loader, url) warms the cache before mount.

When a loader result has .scene, useLoader also returns { nodes, materials } keyed by name, which is what gltfjsx output consumes. For any other Object3D, useGraph(object) builds the same memoized collection.
replaces: scene.traverse to find a named mesh

recipe: State read inside useFrame is the live frame state, delivered fresh each frame without re-rendering; state read during render is a snapshot that only updates when the store notifies. Prefer the former for anything animated.

v9 ordering: callbacks run in ascending priority. A negative priority orders a callback early without taking over rendering; any positive priority disables r3f's automatic render and makes you responsible for gl.render.

v10 replaces priority with named phases: start, input, physics, update (default), render, finish. Order across packages with before/after on a job id or phase name, because a bare number cannot compose between libraries that both pick 0.

To add render work in v10 without taking over, use { before: 'render' } or { after: 'render' } instead of { phase: 'render' }. The built-in render still runs and several components can compose around it.

v10's useFrame returns controls: pause, resume, step, stepAll, invalidate, id, rootId, and a reactive isPaused backed by useSyncExternalStore. Calling useFrame() with no callback is the sanctioned way to reach the scheduler without registering a job.

v10's useFrame no longer throws outside <Canvas>. It lazily creates an ambient scheduler root and the callback gets timing only ({ time, delta, elapsed, frame }) with no gl/scene/camera. A later Canvas adopts those jobs.

Reach v10's scheduler via useThree().scheduler, useFrame() with no callback, the frame state, or getScheduler() outside React. It is a Symbol.for singleton, so mixing '@react-three/fiber' and '/webgpu' imports still yields one loop, and it survives HMR.

frameloop="never" stops the loop entirely; step frames with advance(timestamp), scheduler.step(), or the stepAll from useFrame controls. That is the mode for deterministic tests and offline/non-realtime rendering.

useGLTF(url) defaults useDraco and useMeshOpt to true, pulling DRACO decoders from the gstatic CDN only for compressed models. Self-host with useGLTF(url, '/draco-gltf') or globally via useGLTF.setDecoderPath. Warm the cache with useGLTF.preload(url) at module scope.

For loaders the model needs beyond draco, use the fourth extendLoader argument rather than a bespoke useLoader call, so the cache stays shared: useGLTF(url, true, true, loader => loader.setKTX2Loader(ktx2.detectSupport(gl))).

<Environment preset="city" /> fetches HDRIs from a GitHub-hosted CDN; drei says explicitly it is not meant for production and may fail. Ship the file yourself with files=, or dynamically import @pmndrs/assets so it stays out of the main bundle.

Environment with children renders them into an off-buffer and films one cube-camera frame, so it is cheap. Only add frames={Infinity} when the environment must animate, and drop resolution (256 or less) when you do.

drei controls damp by default, drive their own updates, clean up on unmount, and already invalidate under frameloop="demand" — do not wire that yourself. They deliberately run before every other useFrame so your code can override the camera.

makeDefault publishes the instance to state.controls, which is what CameraShake, GizmoHelper, TransformControls and Bounds look for. Camera controls follow whichever camera has makeDefault; pass camera= only for a non-default one.
replaces: passing controls refs down through props

recipe: <Instances> keeps component ergonomics at one draw call, but each <Instance> carries real CPU overhead. Past a few thousand items, or for foliage, drop to a raw THREE.InstancedMesh. limit sizes the buffer, range the draw range.

An <Instance> binds to its nearest <Instances> provider, so two instanced types in one subtree collide. createInstances() returns a dedicated provider/instance pair per type, and takes a generic for typed custom attributes.
replaces: nesting two <Instances> and hoping the pairing works

recipe: Custom per-instance shader attributes go through <InstancedAttribute name="foo" defaultValue={1} />, which allocates and updates the buffer; then set foo={10} on each Instance. defaultValue may be a float or an array for wider strides.

When the repeated objects are already-loaded meshes rather than JSX geometry, use <Merged meshes={nodes}>, which yields one component per mesh through a render prop and costs exactly one draw call per type.

<Html> occlude takes true, a ref array, or "blending" for real depth occlusion — but blending only occludes rectangular elements unless you pass a matching geometry prop. On hide it sets opacity on the innermost div; onOcclude to animate it.

Html transform mode renders via matrix3d and looks blurry on some browsers. The documented mitigation is to scale the Html parent down and scale the inner div back up: <Html transform scale={0.5}><div style={{transform:'scale(2)'}}/>.

Two cheap raycast fixes before optimising anything else: raycast={meshBounds} for bounds-only hit testing when precision does not matter, and <Bvh firstHitOnly> around a subtree, which builds boundsTree and reverts cleanly when unmounted.

Materials compile lazily when they first enter the frustum, which jerks the first camera move. <Preload all /> inside the model's Suspense boundary calls gl.compile up front; without all it only precompiles currently visible objects.

AdaptiveDpr and AdaptiveEvents are the consumers of state.performance.current; they do nothing unless something calls regress() (drei controls have a regress flag). AdaptiveDpr pixelated is cheaper still. BakeShadows freezes shadow maps at mount.

PerformanceMonitor averages fps and calls onIncline/onDecline outside your bounds. Set factor to where you start (0 lowest, 1 highest, 0.5 default) and use flipflops + onFallback to pin a baseline; after fallback it shuts down.
SoftShadows injects PCSS into three's shader chunks, so mounting or unmounting it recompiles every shader in the scene. Mount it with the rest of the scene; toggling it at runtime is a visible stall.

MeshTransmissionMaterial costs an extra scene pass per material and temporarily removes its host mesh from the render stack. With roughness a 32x32 resolution still looks right. Share cost via transmissionSampler or one buffer, accepting that materials stop seeing each other.

<View> scissors one canvas into several viewports tied to tracking divs — the right answer to "many canvases on one page". Put <View.Port /> inside the Canvas and reconnect eventSource to a parent wrapping both canvas and DOM.

Each <Hud> is an isolated portal scene with its own camera that takes over rendering. The first one must have renderPriority 1 because it clears and draws the default scene; be explicit about priorities when stacking several.

<Clone object={nodes.table} /> shallow-clones an Object3D and keeps referencing the original geometries and materials, so reuse is free. deep can be true, 'materialsOnly' or 'geometriesOnly'; inject swaps materials across every mesh inside.
replaces: adding the same loaded object twice

recipe: <Text> is troika SDF text and suspends while the font loads. Pass characters="..." with the glyphs you actually use to avoid a flash of unstyled text. All troika props pass through.

<Bounds fit clip observe> frames the scene and needs makeDefault on your camera controls. useBounds() gives refresh().clip().fit(); refresh recomputes the box, so call it only when the view really changed. With orthographic cameras fit() only zooms: add reset() to center.
_original_recipe: <Bounds fit clip observe> frames the scene and needs makeDefault on your controls. useBounds() gives refresh().clip().fit(); refresh recomputes the box, so call it only when the view really changed. Orthographic cameras need reset(), not fit().
_review_reason: drei docs: for ortho cameras fit() only zooms, reset() centers; example chains refresh().reset().clip().fit(), not 'reset instead of fit'

recipe: React context does not cross the Canvas reconciler boundary. useContextBridge(ThemeContext, ...) forwards providers that already sit above the bridging component — you cannot render the providers inside the component that calls the hook.

drei v11 splits entry points. Cameras, controls, staging, loaders and hooks stay at the root and are renderer-agnostic; materials, render targets (Fbo, RenderTexture, CubeCamera) and effects must come from '/legacy' or '/webgpu'. Root import defaults to WebGL.
source_name: drei v10 to v11 Migration Guide

recipe: drei v11 is ESM-only with no CJS bundle, and requires r3f v10 even for pure WebGL projects because it depends on v10's scheduler and node integration throughout. Jest setups need ESM config or a move to Vitest.
source_name: drei v10 to v11 Migration Guide

recipe: drei v11 alpha's WebGPU port is incomplete: the maintainers say a file under src/webgpu does not mean the component works, and materials can look different between the /legacy and /webgpu builds. Verify each WebGPU component before relying on it.
source_name: drei v10 to v11 Migration Guide
_original_recipe: drei v11's WebGPU port is incomplete; maintainers warn a file under src/webgpu does not mean the component works. Materials are known to render differently between the WebGL and WebGPU builds. Alpha.7 tracks three 0.185.1 and r3f 10.0.0-alpha.4.
_review_reason: 'alpha.7 tracks three 0.185.1 and r3f alpha.4' not supported by the migration doc (alpha.7 is a future milestone there); volatile version pin removed

recipe: <Detailed distances={[0,10,20]}> wraps THREE.LOD; children go highest quality first and the distance array must match them one to one. Cheapest win when vertex count, not draw calls, is the bottleneck.

useTexture takes a url, an array, or a key/url record that spreads straight onto a material: const props = useTexture({ map, metalnessMap }); <meshStandardMaterial {...props} />. It is useLoader + TextureLoader, so the same cache applies.

In v9 WebGPU is manual: the gl prop may return a promise, so gl={async props => { const r = new WebGPURenderer(props); await r.init(); return r }}, plus extend(THREE) from 'three/webgpu' and ThreeToJSXElements for the node-material JSX.
In v10 the whole v9 WebGPU dance collapses to <Canvas renderer>. R3F calls init() for you, and renderer also accepts a config bag or a pre-created instance. No awaited factory, no manual extend.
replaces: gl={async props => { const r = new WebGPURenderer(props); await r.init(); return r }}

recipe: The '@react-three/fiber/webgpu' entry auto-extends the THREE WebGPU namespace, so <meshStandardNodeMaterial /> resolves without a manual extend call. It also narrows useThree and useFrame to WebGPURootState, removing the instanceof casts v9 needed.
replaces: extend(THREE as any) for node materials

recipe: WebGPURenderer is the TSL renderer, not a backend gate; it runs on WebGL too. renderer={{ forceWebGL: true }} keeps node materials and TSL on a WebGL backend. R3F names the split by renderer, not backend: 'renderer' versus 'legacy'.

'three' and 'three/webgpu' are different bundles, not flavours. R3F resolves each entry through one internal alias so a /webgpu build never pulls the WebGL renderer in and /legacy never pulls WebGPU in. Mixing entries defeats that.

useUniforms, useNodes, useLocalNodes, useRenderPipeline, useBuffers and useGPUStorage exist only on '@react-three/fiber/webgpu' and only in v10. Importing them from the root or legacy entry is a v9-trained model's most likely fabrication.

The rule that governs everything: JavaScript if/else/for inside a node creator runs once at graph-build time and can never react to a uniform. Use TSL If()/ElseIf()/select() for anything that must branch per frame on the GPU.

Before creating a uniform, check for a TSL built-in: time, cameraPosition, cameraViewMatrix and friends already exist, so mirroring state.camera or driving a uTime by hand is redundant. Reserve uniforms for things with no node, like size and dpr.

Update uniform values imperatively in useFrame — uTime.value = elapsed — never through setState. TSL nodes reference the uniform object, so a value change never rebuilds the graph and never re-renders React.

useNodes is cached forever and is for expensive shared work (noise functions, shared varyings). useLocalNodes is component-local and re-runs only when a uniform, node or texture is added or removed — never on a value change.

All creator hooks are create-if-not-exists, so calling useUniforms({ uTime: 0 }) in several components reuses one GPU allocation and is StrictMode-safe. Pass a scope name to keep the same key independent per feature: useUniforms({ uHealth: 100 }, 'player').

three renamed PostProcessing to RenderPipeline in r183, and R3F followed: usePostProcessing was a public export at alpha.2 and no longer exists. The store key moved too, from state.postProcessing to state.renderPipeline.

useRenderPipeline callbacks deliberately do not re-run on hot reload, because rebuilding them corrupts TSL state. Edits to a pipeline need an explicit rebuild() or a full page reload; uniforms, nodes, buffers and storage do rebuild atomically.

WebGPU canvases can share one renderer and GPU context: <Canvas id="main" renderer> plus <Canvas renderer={{ primaryCanvas: 'main', scheduler: { after: 'main', fps: 30 } }}>. Each keeps its own scene, camera, events and store, reached via primaryStore.

Scoped names from useUniforms, useNodes, useBuffers and useGPUStorage become WGSL identifiers. Since alpha.4 R3F sanitizes them, but keep scope and key names identifier-safe anyway: spaces, punctuation and leading digits produced invalid struct declarations before that.

R3F trails three by design. v10 requires three >=0.185 precisely because it consumes three's own RenderPipeline, CubeRenderTarget and UniformNode types instead of shadowing them; v9 accepts three >=0.156 but ships no WebGPU or TSL hooks at all.

Alpha.5 removed R3F's stale ShaderNodeObject and three/tsl Fn augmentations, so three's own Fn overloads (including the Fn(fn, 'void') statement form compute kernels use) work again with R3F installed. Earlier alphas needed casts.

useBuffers wraps compute buffers (TypedArray, BufferAttribute, StorageBufferAttribute, instancedArray/storage nodes) and useGPUStorage wraps StorageTexture/Storage3DTexture, both scoped and create-if-not-exists. Both are marked experimental and their surface is still moving.
